items.title: Benghazi drone attack: Is Ukraine opening a Mediterranean front against Russia?
items.content:
Benghazi drone attack: Is Ukraine opening a Mediterranean front against Russia?
Submitted by
Omar Ashour
on
Mon, 11/23/2026 - 11:54
The strategic test is whether repeated attacks constrain Moscow’s ability to sustain its war and overseas military deployments
A satellite image shows smoke rising from a burning ship in the Libyan port of Benghazi. Ukraine claimed it was behind strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on 23 November, 2026 (AFP)
Off
On Monday, hours after
Ukraine
claimed
responsibility for the drone attack that sank Russian warship at
Libyan
naval base, Ukraine Security Service (SBU)
said
in a statement that "Russia’s military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes even far beyond the Black Sea."
The wreckage at Benghazi gave that warning substance.
Kyiv says seven Ukrainian naval drones
sank
the Russian corvette Merkury, destroyed its Ka-27 helicopter and also struck the weapons transport ship MV Angara.
Satellite imagery
showed
the corvette capsized. Commissioned in 2023, Merkury was a modern combatant, designed to fight ships and submarines and defend against air attack. Ukraine - a country
deprived of most of its conventional navy
as of 2014 following Russia's annexation of Crimea - is extending maritime attrition into Russia’s Mediterranean foothold in 2026.
As
previously argued
in Middle East Eye, maritime denial can defeat a superior navy’s strategic objectives without winning conventional fleet battles.
Benghazi is the latest proof.
A campaign across seas
The 11 named vessels in Ukrainian-claimed or suspected incidents since August 2025 illustrate four overlapping target sets. The first is "sea combatants", exemplified by Merkury.
The second is "military transport": Angara was struck near Benghazi while
Sparta II
was hit in the Gulf of Finland while bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. Neither a warship nor a naval supply carrier should be casually conflated with an oil tanker or the "shadow fleet". That is a different category.
The Caspian gamble: Iran-Ukraine tensions widen the 'geography of instability'
Read More »
The third is "commercial ships" that carry military cargo. Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces
struck
Port Olya-4 in August 2025, saying it carried Iranian Shahed components and ammunition through the Caspian corridor.
The Russian freighter Lady Mariia was reportedly
attacked
between Crete and Libya in September.
Fourth is the "tanker war": Russian tankers struck include
Kairos, Virat
and Dashan in the Black Sea, and Qendil in the Mediterranean, alongside suspected operations against the LNG carrier
Arctic Metagaz
and
Mersin off Senegal
.
This is a minimum illustrative count, not a comprehensive set of confirmed Ukrainian successes.
Kyiv’s "long-range sanctions" seek military enforcement against Russia’s military naval assets and sanctions-evading energy trade. The operational objective appears to be cumulative attrition: destroy fighting platforms, interrupt deliveries, and force Russia to disperse scarce protection assets.
The strategic test is whether repeated attacks constrain Moscow’s ability to sustain its war and overseas military deployments. A sustained campaign would require repeated replenishment of drones, munitions, fuel and spare parts as well as political access and legitimacy in the form of consent from host governments for any use of their ports, coastal facilities or territorial waters
alongside successful strikes.
By late October, the Black Sea was
called
"the world’s deadliest shipping route", with more than 570 vessels struck during 2026 and at least 40 seafarers killed, against 24 killed in Hormuz.
Russia’s attacks have again
strangled
Ukrainian grain exports and compromised international food security, making Kyiv's maritime resistance an economic necessity.
The theatre linkage between the Baltic, Black Sea, the Mediterranean and the Gulf recalls Soviet military thinking about mutually supporting fronts, without implying a single formal theatre.
Russia’s own
2022 maritime doctrine
places Baltic, Black Sea and Mediterranean priorities within its Atlantic regional military direction.
For example, since Moscow’s 2015 Syrian intervention, the multi-front pressure in
Syria
and Ukraine
have been interacting
. Kyiv is turning that geographical multi-front logic against Russia.
Hybrid defence
Ukraine’s military intelligence, HUR, operates
Magura drones
. The V5’s specifications include an 800km range and 320kg payload capacity. HUR says
six V5 strikes
sank the missile boat Ivanovets in February 2024. The newer V7 carries missiles and has
reportedly downed
Su-30 fighters.
Benghazi’s wider significance lies in how far a weaker navy can now reach - and how much a stronger one must spend to contain it
These are evolving combat platforms, alongside expendable explosive boats. Their effect is to make protection more demanding for a larger navy, which must defend its ships against threats above and below the horizon.
Benghazi’s drone model remains officially undisclosed at the time of writing. But the sustained distant operations require access, intelligence and replenishment as much as impressive range figures.
One successful raid cannot establish that these requirements are permanently secured. Strategically, this is how hybrid defence works:
conventional and unconventional means integrated
across domains.
Ukraine draws on land, sea, air, space, information, electronic and cyber capabilities. The precise combination in Benghazi remains undisclosed. An earlier
MEE analysis
of Ukraine’s drone revolution stressed that institutional adaptation converts technology into sustained military effectiveness.
Crimea: The beginning and the end
Russia’s war began in Crimea, and the war is already back in Crimea. It will likely end in Crimea.
The peninsula lies roughly 300km across the Black Sea from Turkey’s Sinop and slightly over 1,800km from Benghazi. The latter distance once offered Moscow sanctuary.
Iran and the Houthis have reason to study that model closely, with implications for shipping protection from the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea
Ukraine’ impressive reach is eroding it.
Tobruk and Benghazi are possible footholds for Russia amid uncertainty over Syria's Tartus. Hence, striking escorts and transports could raise basing costs, interrupt military deliveries and burden protection forces.
Russia’s Africa Corps and
Wagner-linked networks
connect Libya with conflicts farther south.
Twelve ships
were accused of providing military deliveries to Africa, including routes from Kaliningrad to Libya. Disrupting these connections will affect Russia’s staying power across several theatres.
And Ukraine has concrete national security interests here. Wagner helped devastate Bakhmut, where its late chief Prigozhin acknowledged losing around
20,000 fighters
. US sanctions
trace
illicit gold revenues funding operations in Ukraine (and Africa). Kyiv believes that disrupting that network serves Ukrainian national security and defence.
Benghazi is another demonstration of the new and enhanced naval warfare: smaller forces projecting combat power across seas through intelligence, forward access and relatively inexpensive uncrewed systems.
The operational test is whether Ukraine can turn distant raids into a sustained campaign that forces Russia to disperse escorts, reinforce ports and reconsider basing arrangements.
Iran and the Houthis have reason to study that model closely, with implications for shipping protection from the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea.
Benghazi’s wider significance lies in how far a weaker navy can now reach - and how much a stronger one must spend to contain it.

items.title: Iran carries out flogging of singer and her team, Iranian website says
items.content:
DUBAI, Nov 23 (Reuters) - An Iranian singer and four members of her production team have each received 74 lashes after being sentenced for "offending public decency by producing and publishing obscene and immoral content online", an Iranian news website said on Monday.
Parastoo Ahmadi and the four others were also handed two-year bans on artistic and musical activities and travel, the Emtedad website quoted lawyer Mostafa Nili as saying.

items.title: US imposes sanctions on dozens linked to Iran's shadow banking networks
items.content:
By Andrea Shalal
WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - The Trump administration has issued new Iran-related sanctions targeting dozens of people and entities, the Treasury Department said on Monday, stepping up its effort to isolate Iran from the global economy and disrupt its shadow banking networks.
Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) also released an analysis identifying nearly $15 billion of financial activity conducted from January 2025 to August 2026 that it said was potentially linked to Iranian shadow banking.

items.title: Federal court clears way for army to detonate bomb-making chemicals in Iowa
items.content:
Trump, on social media, tried to push responsibility of ‘any and all death or destruction’ on Democratic governor-elect
The US army can proceed with detonating several tons of degraded bomb-making chemicals in Iowa, a federal appeals court ruled on Monday. The order came after a day of uncertainty that saw Donald Trump attempt to foist responsibility “for any and all death or destruction” on Iowa’s Democratic governor-elect Rob Sands.
The detonation of 68 barrels containing nearly 9,500lb of lead azide was initially planned for Friday, but the army has since changed the date three times after an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.
